Norfolk by Motorcycle: Big Skies and Empty Beaches

Norfolk won't win awards for dramatic mountain passes or hairpin bends, but it offers something equally valuable — space, tranquillity, and some of the biggest skies in England. The Norfolk coast is a succession of marshes, sandy beaches, and handsome flint villages that feels worlds away from the rest of southern England.

The Coast Road

The A149 from King's Lynn to Cromer is Norfolk's signature ride. It follows the coast through Hunstanton (one of the few east coast towns with a west-facing beach), through the beautiful villages of Burnham Market, Wells-next-the-Sea, and Blakeney, to the Victorian resort of Cromer. The road is straight and flowing — perfect for relaxed touring.

Key Stops Along the Coast

  • Holkham Beach — Vast, cinematic beach backed by pine forests. Park at the car park and walk to the sea
  • Wells-next-the-Sea — Working harbour, excellent fish and chips, miniature railway
  • Blakeney Point — Grey seal colony accessible by boat, spectacular wildlife
  • Cley-next-the-Sea — Famous birdwatching marshes and a beautiful windmill
  • Cromer — Victorian pier, famous for Cromer crab, charming seafront

Inland Norfolk

Turn inland and Norfolk reveals another character. The Broads are a network of rivers and lakes formed from medieval peat excavations. Riding through Broads villages like Horning and Ranworth gives you glimpses of boats and waterways between the hedgerows. The area around Castle Acre and Fakenham is quintessential English countryside with quiet lanes and ancient churches.

Norfolk is flat, but the skies more than compensate. At sunset, the whole coast turns gold and the huge sky fills with colour. It's a photographer's dream.

The Route

Start from King's Lynn and follow the A149 east along the coast to Cromer. Continue south through the Broads via Stalham and Wroxham to Norwich. From Norwich, head west through Swaffham and back to King's Lynn. The complete loop is about 130 miles — perfect for a relaxed day ride with plenty of stops.

Practical Tips

Norfolk is flat — expect wind, especially on exposed coastal sections. The roads are well-maintained but many are straight and can become monotonous if you're used to mountain riding. The compensations are the scenery, the food (Cromer crab, Brancaster mussels, local ale), and the sheer peacefulness. Fuel stations are plentiful throughout Norfolk. Visit in summer for the beaches or autumn for the spectacular migrating bird flocks at Cley and Titchwell marshes.

Key stops include Holkham Beach, Wells-next-the-Sea, Blakeney Point's seal colony and Cley's marshes.

faq.q: What kind of riding does Norfolk offer?
faq.a: Norfolk will not win awards for mountain passes or hairpins, but it offers space, tranquillity and some of the biggest skies in England. The coast is a succession of marshes, sandy beaches and handsome flint villages, so it suits relaxed touring and photography rather than spirited cornering.

faq.q: What is the main coastal route?
faq.a: The A149 from King's Lynn to Cromer is Norfolk's signature ride. It follows the coast through Hunstanton, Burnham Market, Wells-next-the-Sea and Blakeney to the Victorian resort of Cromer. The road is straight and flowing, perfect for relaxed touring with frequent stops at beaches and villages.

faq.q: Is there a good full-day loop?
faq.a: Yes. Start from King's Lynn and follow the A149 east to Cromer, then head south through the Broads via Stalham and Wroxham to Norwich, before returning west through Swaffham to King's Lynn. The complete loop is about 130 miles, ideal for a relaxed day with plenty of stops.

Visit in summer for the beaches or autumn for the spectacular migrating bird flocks at Cley and Titchwell marshes. Norfolk is flat, so expect wind on exposed coastal sections, but fuel stations are plentiful throughout. The compensations are the scenery, the local food and the sheer peacefulness.
